Charge Carriers in a Conductor

A metal wire holds an enormous number of free electrons — about one per atom in copper. Three quantities describe it:

  • Number density \(n\): mobile carriers per unit volume (m\(^{-3}\))
  • Carrier charge \(q\): for electrons, \(|q| = e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C
  • Cross-sectional area \(A\) (m\(^2\))

Current from Drift Velocity

The carriers move along the wire with an average drift velocity \(v_d\).

Step 1 — the swept volume. In time \(\Delta t\) each carrier advances \(\Delta x = v_d\Delta t\), so every carrier within that distance of a cross-section crosses it. That region is a cylinder of volume \(Av_d\Delta t\).

Step 2 — count the carriers. At \(n\) per unit volume, the cylinder holds \(N = nAv_d\Delta t\) carriers.

Step 3 — the charge. Each carries \(q\): \(\Delta Q = Nq = nqAv_d\Delta t\).

Step 4 — divide by \(\Delta t\).

\[\boxed{\;I = nqv_dA\;}\]

Dividing by the area gives the current density, the current per unit area:

\[\vec J = nq\vec v_d, \qquad J = \frac{I}{A}\]

\(\vec J\) is a vector that points along the flow of positive charge. For electrons \(q<0\), so \(\vec v_d\) and \(\vec J\) point in opposite directions — the electrons drift against the current, as §26.1 said.

Random Motion vs. Drift

With no applied field the free electrons are far from stationary. They move at thermal speeds of order \(10^6\) m/s, but in random directions, so their average velocity is zero and no charge is transported. An applied field \(\vec E\) exerts \(\vec F = q\vec E\) on each electron, biasing its motion slightly between collisions with the lattice. The result is a small drift superimposed on the random motion.

Example: Drift Speed in a Copper Wire

A 12-gauge copper wire (\(A = 3.31 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)) carries \(I = 10.0\) A. Copper has mass density \(\rho_m = 8920\) kg/m\(^3\) and molar mass \(M = 0.0635\) kg/mol, with one free electron per atom.

Step 1 — the carrier density. One electron per atom, so \(n\) is the number density of atoms:

\[n = \frac{N_A\rho_m}{M} = \frac{(6.022 \times 10^{23})(8920)}{0.0635} = 8.46 \times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}\]

Step 2 — solve \(I = nqv_dA\) for the drift speed.

\[v_d = \frac{I}{nqA} = \frac{10.0}{(8.46 \times 10^{28})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(3.31 \times 10^{-6})}\]

\[\boxed{\;v_d = 2.23 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s} \approx 0.223\ \text{mm/s}\;}\]

Check the scale. That is billions of times slower than the thermal motion, and an electron would need about 75 minutes to drift the length of a 1 m wire. Yet a light comes on the instant the switch closes. What travels fast is the field, not the electrons: closing the switch establishes the field along the whole wire at nearly the speed of light, and every electron in the circuit starts drifting almost at once.

*Personal note: Think of a garden hose already full of water. Open the nozzle and water leaves the far end immediately — not because any molecule travelled the length of the hose, but because the pressure wave did.

Example: A Wire That Narrows

A copper wire of diameter \(2.00\) mm is joined to a section of diameter \(1.00\) mm, and the pair carries \(I = 4.00\) A. Find the drift speed and the current density in each section. (\(n = 8.46 \times 10^{28}\) m\(^{-3}\).)

Step 1 — one current. By the check in §26.1, both sections carry the same \(I = 4.00\) A. Only the area changes.

Step 2 — the areas. \(A_1 = \pi(1.00 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 3.14 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\) and \(A_2 = \pi(0.500 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 7.85 \times 10^{-7}\) m\(^2\).

Step 3 — drift speed and current density.

\[v_{d1} = \frac{I}{nqA_1} = \frac{4.00}{(8.46 \times 10^{28})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(3.14 \times 10^{-6})} = 9.39 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s}\]

\[J_1 = \frac{I}{A_1} = 1.27 \times 10^{6}\ \text{A/m}^2\]

Halving the diameter quarters the area, so without recomputing:

\[\boxed{\;v_{d2} = 4v_{d1} = 3.76 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s}, \qquad J_2 = 4J_1 = 5.09 \times 10^{6}\ \text{A/m}^2\;}\]

Check against continuity. \(A_1v_{d1} = A_2v_{d2}\), exactly the fluid result \(A_1v_1 = A_2v_2\) — the electrons speed up through the narrow section the way water speeds up through a nozzle. The narrow section needs four times the current density, so it will also need four times the field; §26.3 shows why, and why that section is where a wire heats first.
